cards.jan-craig: Jan was an avid golfer who could not find covers she liked, so she knitted her own on a rural route outside Cincinnati, shared party line and all. Jack Nicklaus ordered a set in the mid-sixties, and Tom Watson and multiple Ryder Cup teams carried them after him. They are still hand-knit to order in 100% worsted wool, $63 to $79, and the only design change in six decades was elastic inside the driver covers.
cards.seamus: A Royal Troon headcover Akbar had been given wore out in 2011, and Megan, a womenswear designer at Pendleton Woolen Mills, rebuilt it in a garage from factory remnants. The company is made of Pendleton scrap, and Pendleton became a licensed partner rather than the other way round. The first order was Bandon Dunes. Covers run $110 to $140 in wool, leather, waxed canvas and tweed, and the company registers as women and minority owned.
cards.bluetross: Marc wanted to turn a pin flag from Newport Country Club into a headcover for his brother, and the flag still hangs unmade in the production facility while the company it accidentally spawned sells $225 versions of the idea. The first prototypes came off Gail’s inherited sewing machine, which Marc destroyed inside a month. Italian vachetta and Horween leather patina rather than wear out, and the range runs to belts, wallets and scorecard covers.
cards.daphnes: Daphne’s invented the animal headcover and made Frank, the tiger Tiger Woods first carried at the 1997 Masters, after which business grew 400% in a quarter. Nike licensed the character and named him; Spicer’s one condition was that he stay likable, because her late mother’s actual signature is stitched into the label of every cover the company makes. A hundred-plus designs sit at a flat $45.99, from wolf and shark to Nicklaus’s Golden Bear.
cards.mackem: Mackem is slang for a native of Sunderland, which is where Adam is from. Paige has the textiles background and does the pattern-making and construction, and Adam calls her the brains and the brawn of it. Everything is cut and sewn in their own Kalamunda studio in wool, houndstooth, corduroy, waxed canvas and tartan, with a further line built from reclaimed materials. Covers run A$85 to A$95, pouches to A$125.
cards.zaleas: Zalea’s does not market to men at all. The homepage reads Headcovers Made for HER GAME and every description names a lady golfer, but the gingham and stripe patterns are neutral enough to sit on anyone’s bag. It started as a dorm-room Etsy shop and the covers are still cut by Zoe’s mother and sewn by her grandmother, with every print drawn by Zoe herself. Twice a year the scrap becomes one-off covers, at $70.
cards.orkai: Deborah Bennett is CEO and Erica Bennett president and chief designer, and they built it together. ORKAI was official bag supplier to all eight teams at the 2023 LPGA International Crown, hand-finished in Boca Raton in vegan Nappa rather than hide. They rebranded from ORCA Golf in January 2026 to push into travel and lifestyle, keeping the orca’s fluke as the mark because no two are alike. Bags start at $275, bespoke commissions to $1,580.
cards.hedge: Hedge came out of frustration with kit designed mostly by men, on a tennis court at the Bridgehampton Club; Ouderkirk came from Ralph Lauren. The range is the strangest in golf: a $99.99 Sunday bag and $29.99 Cabretta gloves next to a caddie brooch and a stroke-counter bracelet handmade by a named jeweller. Their Criquet collab began as a joke at the 2018 PGA Show about the two brands dating, made real a year later.
cards.sinking-birdies: The prints are bold graphics on the things you lose: AAA Cabretta gloves at £18, magnetic microfibre towels, PU driver and mallet covers, bamboo tees and a leather glove case, with no florals anywhere. The brand’s own site names no founder, and neither does the one piece of UK trade press about it. Christina Rogers is on record in exactly one place, a Companies House filing dated 4 July 2023, the day it incorporated.
cards.devant: Mary Ann started Devant in 1976 by taking the small short-run orders a big contract mill could not be bothered with. It now makes over a million towels a year in Pageland, South Carolina, under USGA, PGA of America, PGA Tour and LPGA licences, so the towel on the bag at the U.S. Open traces back to her. Fifty years of continuous trading is close to unheard of for a woman-founded hard-goods company.
cards.inside-story: Shee was a college golfer at UC Riverside and then UNLV, and picked up the nickname Sock Girl for wearing over-the-knee socks as sun protection, a teenage workaround for her mother’s sunscreen rules. She co-founded the company in 2019 with Greg Ashton and her mother Kat. The yarn is nano-particled coffee grounds plus recycled bottle fibre, about 70% upcycled, and carries a four-year no-hole guarantee. Men’s crew and calf start at $18.
cards.kingfisher: Cohen is a woman designing men’s clothes, with no women’s line at all. She was an art director at PepsiCo before she started Kingfisher at a kitchen counter in East Dallas with a sewing machine and thrift-store fabric. Tees are screen-printed at a shop in Old East Dallas at $40; the $65 polos come from the same factories as the big performance brands. Its breakout was a citywide open call to find Dallas’s worst golfer.
cards.rhoback: Kristina was the first of the three to go full time, spending the brand’s first two years towing a pop-up cross-country and selling shirts out of parking lots, 25,000 miles of it. She built the original website, teaching herself the software to do it. The name comes from their Rhodesian Ridgeback, and the two vertical stripes on the back of every piece are the ridge. Men’s performance polos are $98, vests $154, quarter-zips $145.
cards.malbon: Malbon began as an Instagram mood board, and Erica arrived having co-founded The Now, an LA massage business, with no background in sport or retail. The brand launched menswear first in 2017 and did not add a proper women’s line until 2023; by her own account men’s is where the market was. She is co-chief creative officer today, a title she kept when an outside CEO arrived. Tees are $68, polos $108 to $148.
cards.bunker-mentality: Bunker Mentality has been independent for more than twenty years, which almost nothing in the category manages. The interesting part is recent: they abandoned stocked inventory and moved to made-to-order, so each garment is printed, cut and sewn only once you have bought it and ships straight from a UK factory, which leaves no warehouse and no discount cycle. Twenty-four sizes across three body lengths come as standard; men’s polos are £70, gilets £110.
cards.royal-albartross: Alex Bartholomew built one of very few luxury footwear houses in golf founded by a woman, and she trained for it: fashion and textiles at Brighton, shoemaking at Cordwainers, LK Bennett, Burberry and the British Leather Technology Centre. The shoes are made in small family-run factories in Italy and Portugal on Vibram soles. The name is a love letter in plain sight: Al Bart for Alex Bartholomew, Ross for her husband, around the golf term.
cards.duca-del-cosma: Antje Elle trained at the Munich School for Fashion Graphic Design and co-founded Duca del Cosma in 2004 with the Venetian designer Baldovino Mattiazzo; the name means Duke of Cosma, from his family. Neither owns it now: a Dutch shoe-industry veteran bought it around 2015, a Dubai investment firm in May 2026. A house selling twenty years of Italian heritage has not been owned by either founder for a decade; men’s shoes start at $100.

kickers.1: These are the brands where a woman is the one cutting and sewing the product: a hand-knitting operation running since 1962, a Pendleton designer working in factory scrap, and a leather shop built on an inherited sewing machine.
kickers.2: These are the things that hang off the bag or go in it. Two have been trading since the seventies, and one names no founder anywhere on its own site, leaving a Companies House filing as the only public record.
kickers.3: These brands cut an actual men’s line. One of them sells nothing else, one started as a camper towed across America, and one is an Italian shoe house that has not been owned by its founders for a decade.
